jobs.text: According to the Mahaabhaarat, this serpent was used as a rope... to turn a mountain taller than ten Earths, stacked on top of each other.
This is Vaasuki, king of the serpents, who coils around Lord Shiva's neck.
The dayvaas and the asuraas sought amrit, the nectar of immortality, hidden within the ocean of milk.
To churn it out, they used Mount Mandaraa as the churning rod, and Vaasuki as the rope.
The dayvaas held one end. The asuraas held the other.
The Mahaabhaarat says Mandaraa rose eleven thousand yojanaas above the ground.
If one yojanaa is about thirteen kilometres, that's around a hundred and forty-three thousand kilometres. More than eleven Earths stacked up.
The mountain was so heavy it began to sink. So Vishnu became Koorma, a giant tortoise, and held it on his back.
And Vaasuki had to coil around its entire height.
Even if Mandaraa were only as wide as Earth, one single coil would be forty thousand kilometres long. The entire equator.
As they churned, poison poured out. Lord Shiva drank it to save the world, and it turned his throat blue.
In Baanka, Bihar, stands a granite hill called Mandaar. Spiral grooves run around it, which local tradition attributes to Vaasuki.
Follow for more of India's epics, measured at real scale.
